Mipham's buddha-nature as the union of luminosity and emptiness corresponds to the awareness Dzogchen introduces; partial because the sūtra term names the potential, the Dzogchen term the recognized presence
Both name the root ignorance of saṃsāra; Dzogchen specifies it as non-recognition of the ground's display (Tsigdön Dzöd topic 2)
Longchenpa's all-base is the basis of karmic traces, like the Yogācāra ālaya, but kept distinct from the all-base consciousness
Bön's kun gzhi is the ultimate ground; the Nyingma kun gzhi is not — the equivalence holds only across the two traditions' vocabularies and is contested
The bardo of becoming corresponds to the intermediate existence between death and birth; the six-bardo scheme extends the word to life, dream, meditation, dying and dharmatā
The ground luminosity introduced at death is described as one's own awareness, empty and luminous — the luminous mind of the sūtras
Bön's three-body scheme parallels the Buddhist trikāya; Bön insists on its own lineage for the scheme
Mipham reads buddha-nature as luminosity-emptiness with qualities spontaneously present — the same terms in which Longchenpa describes the ground
The Nyingthig explains the three aspects of the ground as the ground-state of the three kāyas
The Aspiration's formula summarizes the account of delusion from ground-appearances
Both traditions name the culmination 'non-meditation' (sgom med); correspondence of name and function only
Kunjed Gyalpo ch.33 itself labels the three teachers' separate teachings 'provisional'
Shared ninefold structure culminating in Dzogchen; the lower ways differ in content; Bön rejects derivation from the Nyingma scheme
Mipham's account is a reading of the tathāgatagarbha of the sūtras
The bardo of becoming is the intermediate existence of the Abhidharma, elaborated in tantric instruction
Both the Nyingma and the yoga traditions catalogue signs announcing death
Bön's empty-and-clear base inseparable from awareness plays the role of the Nyingma ground; Bön and Nyingma each reject derivation from the other

The four vidyādhara levels are traditionally matched to the path of seeing (matured), seeing/meditation (power over life, mahāmudrā) and no more learning (spontaneous presence); bands follow that match
The outer preliminaries are entry and turning (B0, karma as ethical foundation B1); refuge B0; bodhicitta and Vajrasattva purification B1; maṇḍala, kusāli and guru yoga preparatory disciplines B2
Introduction to awareness is the Dzogchen 'first seeing' (B5); cutting through and direct crossing are cultivation after seeing (B6); exhaustion in dharmatā is final liberation (B7)
Kunjed Gyalpo ch.44 restricts the effortless teaching to the fortunate and prescribes cause-and-result practice for others
Mipham's two ultimates assign the Gelug negation to the enumerated ultimate and the freedom from extremes to the non-enumerated; the Gelug scholars object to this
